# Why the Quran Says We, He, and I

The charge comes in two forms, and both travel widely. The first asks it as arithmetic. Your book says We created you, We sent down the Reminder, We built the heaven. A plural speaker is plural, so who are the others helping Allah? The second asks it as confusion. The same book keeps switching between We, He, and I, sometimes inside one passage, and a speaker who knows who he is does not keep changing his own pronouns.

Both forms assume one thing, that an Arabic pronoun counts its referents the way an English pronoun does. It does not. Arabic has a standing rule for the exalted speaker, the plural of majesty, and the rule is printed in the grammar books, alive in the poets, and used by the Quran itself for single referents of no theological weight at all. When the Quran means that others act alongside Allah, it names them. When it wants the nearness of answer, it drops the relay and speaks as I. When it describes the Lord for the servant to learn, it says He. One Speaker, and many rooms of speech.

> [!abstract]
> Premise 1: Arabic grammar itself lets one exalted speaker say we of himself alone. Al-Farra, the founder of the Kufan school who died in 207, reads the dying soul's plural to the one God as the Arabs' standing plural for one, set beside the Quran addressing the single Prophet in a plural verb. Al-Tusi's al-Tibyan states it as the linguists' answer and relays al-Khalil ibn Ahmad, the founder of Arabic grammar, declining to force a parse on that same plural because it is a plural. Al-'Ukbari's grammar of the Quran reads that verse the same way, with the divine We of Qur'an 15:9 as the parallel. The Shia school states the rule on its own ground, 5:55, where a plural in form has one referent, Ali ﵇ alone.
>
> Premise 2: The usage was alive among the Arabs. Imru' al-Qays says we are the kings and sons of kings. Al-Razi explains the register from the ground up; among the Arabs the great one acts through his household and retinue, so the king says we did, and there is magnification in it. The Prophet ﷺ says we, the company of the prophets. The Imams ﵈ say we of themselves and their house in what the school transmits, and their commentators explain that we with the same device the Quran's shifts use.
>
> Premise 3: The Quran keeps its own naming. It describes the same creation with He in Qur'an 82:7 and with We in Qur'an 95:4, and one hadith proving the Prophet's ﷺ beauty cites both verses side by side. It uses plural forms for single referents elsewhere, a catalogue Ibn Shahrashub drew up from the Quran itself. Where creatures share an act with Allah's permission, the Quran names them, Allah and His angels, the angels and the Spirit by their Lord's permission, and the angels as the addressees, never co-speakers.
>
> Premise 4: The shifts of person are a named device of Arabic eloquence, iltifat, with stated purposes, and the school's own commentary assigns those purposes verse by verse. The Imams ﵈ use the same device in their own speech, and the qudsi reports show Allah answering the servant in His own I where nearness and answer are being promised.

> [!summary]
> Conclusion: if the plural of majesty is ordinary Arabic, and the Quran uses plural forms for single referents and names its co-agents when it has them, then the We carries greatness and never number, and no helper hides inside it. If the person-shifts are a named device the Imams ﵈ themselves use, then the alternation of We, He, and I follows design. The charge survives only by reading an Arabic pronoun as an English census, and that method would convict Genesis and its let-us-make-man verse before it touches the sura of the Reminder.

## 1. The Grammar of the Exalted We

- **Source:** al-Farra, Ma'ani al-Qur'an v2 pp13, 241-242 and v3 p42; al-Tusi, al-Tibyan v7 p394; al-'Ukbari, al-Tibyan fi I'rab al-Qur'an p274; Abu al-Salah al-Halabi, Taqrib al-Ma'arif p188
- **Question:** may one speaker of Arabic say we of himself alone
- **Claim:** the grammar of Arabic has a standing plural of majesty, and it runs in both directions, up to God and down from kings
- **Basis:** the grammarians' verdicts on Qur'an 23:99, 15:9, 23:12, and 6:99, and the school's reading of 5:55

The charge rests on one grammatical assumption, that a pronoun counts its referents. Arabic breaks that assumption before the Quran is even opened. The language has a plural of majesty, a we that one exalted speaker says of himself alone, and the rule is printed in the grammar books with the Quran's own We as the textbook example.

### The Verdict of the Grammarians

> [!tip]- al-Tusi, al-Tibyan, v7, p394
> والثاني - انه جرى على تعظيم الذكر في خطاب الواحد بلفظ الجمع لعظم القدر كما يقول ذلك المتكلم ، قال الله تعالى " انا نحن نزلنا الذكر وانا له لحافظون " (1) وقال " ولقد خلقنا الانسان " (2) وما جرى مجراه . وروى النضر بن سمأل قال : سئل الخليل عن قوله " رب ارجعون " ففكر ثم قال : سألتموني عن شئ لا أحسنه ولا أعرف معناه ، والله أعلم ، لأنه جمع ، فاستحسن الناس منه ذلك
>
> "The second view is that one person is addressed with a plural form to honor the greatness of the one mentioned. A speaker may say this. Allah says, “We sent down the Reminder, and We will preserve it.” He also says, “We created man,” and similar expressions. Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl reported that Khalil was asked about the words, “My Lord, send me back.” He thought for a while and said, “You asked me about something I do not know how to explain, and I do not know its meaning. Allah knows best, since it is plural.” People admired this answer."


So the school's senior classical commentator fixes the rule first. The speech of one speaker can run in the plural form for greatness of station, and he says this is simply how speakers of Arabic talk. His parallel is the charge's own target, the doubled We of the Reminder verse (Qur'an 15:9). The report he relays cuts both ways, and the honest reading records both edges. Al-Khalil ibn Ahmad, a founder of Arabic grammar, was asked about the plural of the dying soul's plea in Qur'an 23:99, send them back, addressed to the one God. He declined to force a parse and said he does not know its analysis, because it is a plural, and the people of his circle found the reserve good. A reader who wants an anomaly can read the reserve his way, and the page does not hide the reserve. The founder's own stated reason is form-side, because it is a plural, and the Kufan school answered him within a generation. That reading is quoted below. The rule of al-Tusi is the tradition's settled answer, the plural of rank where the founder paused, and it runs in both directions, a creature addressing the one God in the plural and God speaking of Himself in it, with neither direction carrying number.

The grammar of the Quran reaches the same verdict in the same breath.

> [!tip]- al-'Ukbari, al-Tibyan fi I'rab al-Qur'an, p274
> * ( ارْجِعُونِ ) * : فيه ثلاثة أوجه :
> أحدها - أنه جمع على التعظيم ، كما قال تعالى : « إِنَّا نَحْنُ نَزَّلْنَا الذِّكْرَ » ، وكقوله : « أَلَمْ تَرَ أَنَّ اللّه أَنْزَلَ مِنَ السَّماءِ ماءً فَأَخْرَجْنا » .
> والثاني - أنه أراد : يا ملائكة ربّي ارجعون .
> والثالث - أنه دلّ بلفظ الجمع على تكرير القول فكأنه قال : ارجعني ارجعنى
>
> "“Send me back” has three explanations. First, it uses the plural to show greatness, as Allah says, “We sent down the Reminder,” and, “Have you not seen that Allah sent water down from the sky, then We brought forth?” Second, it means, “Angels of my Lord, send me back.” Third, the plural shows repeated pleading. It is as if he said, “Send me back, send me back.”"


Al-'Ukbari gives three readings of the plural addressed to God. His first is the plural of magnification, proved from the Reminder verse of Qur'an 15:9 and from a verse that mixes the persons in one sentence, where Allah sends down the water and We brings forth the herbage (Qur'an 6:99), one subject under two grammatical persons, with no second agent named or implied between them. His second reading addresses the plural to the angels, the reading of those who take the number at face value. On that reading the dying soul must be pleading to angels, and the passage gives that plea no support anywhere. The grammar of rank asks for grammar alone, and it is the tradition's answer. The grammarians treat the exalted plural as one fact of the language with two directions. That is the lexical ground the charge never visits.

### The founding school states it plainly

The grammar books cited so far were written in the fifth century and after. Al-Farra stated the rule some three centuries earlier.

> [!tip]- al-Farra, Ma'ani al-Qur'an, v3, p42
> يخاطبون النبي - صلى اللّه عليه - وحده ، وهو كقوله :   « يا أَيُّهَا النَّبِيُّ إِذا طَلَّقْتُمُ النِّساءَ »   (1) في كثير من كلام العرب ، أن تجمع العرب فعل الواحد ، منه قول اللّه ﷿ :  « قالَ رَبِّ ارْجِعُونِ
>
> They address the Prophet alone. It is like His saying, “O Prophet, when you divorce women” (1), in much Arab speech, where the Arabs use the plural form of the verb for one person. Among this is God's saying, “He said, ‘My Lord, send me back.’”

Al-Farra, who died in 207 and took the Kufan school from the generation of al-Kisa'i, the Kufan master reader of the Quran, is commenting on Qur'an 44:36. There the opponents address the Prophet ﷺ alone. He says the plural verb for the one addressee is ordinary Arabic, and his parallel is inside the Quran itself. The sura of divorce opens, O Prophet, when you divorce, with the singular title of honor and the plural verb in one clause (Qur'an 65:1), and the dying soul's send me back (Qur'an 23:99) is, he says, of the same kind. The later tafsir commonly reads the plural of 65:1 as a turn to the community with the Prophet; al-Farra's reading is the Kufan school's own. The book itself addresses one man in the plural and reports one man addressing his one Lord in the plural.

The same grammarian equates the divine Our with the creature's plural in one breath.

> [!tip]- al-Farra, Ma'ani al-Qur'an, v2, p13
> بِأَعْيُنِنا وَوَحْيِنا )  [ 37 ] كقوله  ( ارْجِعُونِ  (7)  )  يخرج على الجمع ومعناه واحد على ما فسّرت لك من قوله  ( بَلْ نَظُنُّكُمْ كاذِبِينَ )  لنوح وحده
>
> “Under Our eyes and by Our revelation” [37], like His saying, “Return” [7], is expressed in the plural although its meaning is singular, according to what I explained to you concerning His saying, “Rather, we think you are liars,” which was addressed to Noah alone.

The ark built under Our eyes and by Our revelation (Qur'an 11:37) is, on al-Farra's gloss, plural in form and singular in meaning, parsed exactly like send me back. And the comparison behind his gloss runs the same way. His earlier reading of rather we think you liars (Qur'an 11:27) took the plural you as addressed to Noah alone, one man receiving the plural of address. The divine We and the creature's exalted plural are one fact of the language to the founding school, not two problems.

And he says so while holding the dying soul's verse in view.

> [!tip]- al-Farra, Ma'ani al-Qur'an, v2, p241
> فجعل الفعل كأنه لجميع (3) وإنما دعا ربه . فهذا ممّا جرى على
>
> So he made the verb as though it were for all (3), though he only called upon his Lord. This is among what occurred according to

> [!tip]- al-Farra, Ma'ani al-Qur'an, v2, p242, continued on the following page
> ما وصف اللّه به نفسه من قوله ( وقد خلقناك (1) من قبل ) في غير مكان من القرآن . فجرى هذا على ذلك
>
> what God described Himself with in His saying, “And We created you (1) before,” in another place of the Quran. This follows that.

The verse runs its verb as though for a plurality, though the dying man called upon his Lord alone, and this, al-Farra says, runs on the same usage as what Allah says of Himself, We created you before (Qur'an 19:9, in his cited reading, where the transmitted text has I created you). The Kufan school had printed the rule with the Quran's own verses generations before the fifth-century glosses, inside the school that grew up around the book's own recitation.

### The School Says It on Its Own Verse

The Shia school states the same rule where its own heart is, the wilaya verse. Qur'an 5:55 says of the one man who gave zakat while bowing, Ali ﵇, in the plural, that they establish the prayer and pay the zakat while bowing. A plural in form, one referent in fact.

> [!tip]- Abu al-Salah al-Halabi, Taqrib al-Ma'arif, p188
> لأن العبارة عن الواحد بلفظ الجمع على جهة التعظيم ظاهر في العربية . وكون علي ﵇ فقيرا غير معلوم
>
> "Arabic clearly uses plural wording for one person to show honor. It is unknown whether Ali was poor."


Abu al-Salah al-Halabi defends that reading by stating the rule as obvious Arabic. Expressing the one by the plural, for magnification, is manifest in the language. The point matters beyond its verse. The school reads the Imam's designation through this grammar, and it stated the rule precisely and early.

> [!tip]- Abu Ali, in Ma'rifa al-Imam, v5, p24
> قال الشيخ أبو عليّ : قال جار الله (2) : إنّما جيء به على لفظ الجمع - وإن كان السبب فيه رجلًا واحداً - ليرغّب الناس في مثل فعله ، ولينبّه أنّ سجيّة المؤمن يجب أن تكون على هذه الغاية من الحرص على البرّ والإحسان . ثمّ قال الشيخ أبو عليّ : وأقول : قد اشتهر في اللغة العبارة عن الواحد بلفظ الجمع للتعظيم ، فلا يحتاج إلى الاستدلال عليه (من قِبل جار الله) .
>
> "Shaykh Abu Ali said that Jar Allah said, "It came in the plural form, though one man caused its revelation, to encourage people to do the same. It also teaches that a believer should be deeply eager for goodness and kindness." Shaykh Abu Ali then said, "Arabic commonly uses plural wording for one person to show honor, so there is no need to prove the point against Jar Allah.""


Abu Ali relays al-Zamakhshari's gloss on 5:55, that the plural form invites every believer to the like of the act, and then goes past it. The rule itself, he says, is too famous in the language to need proof against al-Zamakhshari. The school does not borrow the conclusion from the Sunni philologist. It states the rule to him.

> [!tip]- al-Mar'ashi, Sharh Ihqaq al-Haqq, v3, p587
> نزلنا عنه ، لكن لم لا يجوز أن يكون المراد منه عليا ﵇ ، والواحد قد يعبر عنه بلفظ الجمع ، على سبيل التعظيم كقوله تعالى : إنا أنزلناه في ليلة القدر (1) ، وقال في حق علي ﵇ : والذين يقيمون الصلاة ويؤتون الزكاة وهم راكعون (2)
>
> "We accept that, yet why could it not mean Ali? One person may be described with a plural form to show honor, as Allah says, “We sent it down on the Night of Decree.” He also says about Ali, “Those who establish prayer, give alms, and bow down.”"


Al-Mar'ashi applies the same rule to the divine We itself, the Night of Decree verse (Qur'an 97:1), beside the plural for Ali ﵇. Inside the school, plural-of-majesty for one exalted referent is settled at both ends, God's we and the Imam's they.

The grammar layer closes. The numeric premise of the charge is false as a claim about Arabic.

## 2. How the Kings and Poets Said We

- **Source:** Nashwan al-Himyari, Shams al-'Ulum v3 p287; Lisan al-'Arab v6 p229; al-Razi, Tafsir al-Razi v6 p216; al-Jurjani, al-Hashiya 'ala al-Kashshaf p63
- **Witnesses:** Imru' al-Qays, the raid poet of the Lisan, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, al-Hutay'a
- **Claim:** the exalted we and the shifted person are alive in the usage the dictionaries preserve, at every register from king to prophet

Imru' al-Qays, the most famous poet of the pre-Islamic age, magnifies his royal house in the plural, and every human we in the preserved speech gathers rank around a speaker standing with his people, while the divine We gathers rank without needing any.

> [!quote]- Imru' al-Qays, in Nashwan al-Himyari, Shams al-'Ulum, v3, p287
> نحن الملوك وأبناء الملوك لنا * مُلكٌ به عاش هذا الناسُ أحقابا
>
> *nahnu al-muluku wa-abna'u al-muluki lana / mulkun bihi 'asha hadha al-nasu ahqaba*
>
> "We are kings, sons of kings. Our rule has kept these people alive for ages."


Imru' al-Qays, the most famous poet of the pre-Islamic age, magnifies his royal house in the plural, we the kings and sons of kings. No reader counts the speakers of that line. The line ranks them. Rank is the point, and rank is what the divine We carries. The case of a speaker alone with no house behind him rests with the grammarians, whose rule runs on the plural addressed to the one God, and with the kings' custom, that the king says we of his own command even when his servants carry it out. Al-Razi explains that custom where he is quoted below. The grammarians wrote after the book, and the book is their largest text. The poets and the kings' custom are the evidence no scripture controls, and the verse of the two directions, Qur'an 23:99, is the book meeting the grammarians halfway.

The dictionary's own witnesses carry the same usage at every level of speech.

> [!quote]- Lisan al-'Arab, v6, p229, root n-d-s
> ونَجْرانُ : مدينة بناحية اليمن ؛ يريد أَنهم أَغاروا عليهم عند الصباح ، وتميم بن مر منصوب على الاختصاص لقوله نحن صبحنا ؛ كقول آخر : نَحْنُ بَنِي ضَبَّةَ أَصْحابُ الجَمَل وكقول النبي ، صلى اللّه عليه وسلم : نَحْنُ مَعاشِرَ الأَنْبِياء لا نَرِثُ ولا نُورَثُ
>
> *nahnu sabahna ... nahnu bani Dabbata ashabu al-jamal ... nahnu ma'ashira al-anbiya'i la narithu wa-la nurath*
>
> "Najran is a city near Yemen. He means that they raided its people at dawn. Tamim ibn Murr is in the accusative case for special mention in the phrase, “We raided at dawn.” Another poet said, “We, the sons of Dubba, are the people of the Camel.” The Prophet also said, “We, the community of prophets, neither inherit nor leave inheritance.”"


Three registers in one entry. A tribe's poet says "we struck at dawn" for his people's raid. A house announces itself, "we are the sons of Dubba". And the Prophet ﷺ says "we, the company of the prophets, leave no inheritance", folding the whole company of prophethood into his own we. The pronoun gathers rank around a speaker, and rank has never been a census of who did the deed.

### The Same Art in the Third Person

The charge has a second half, that shifting between persons is confusion. The usage record answers that too, because the poets also speak of themselves in the third person when grandeur calls for it.

> [!tip]- al-Razi, Tafsir al-Razi, v6, p216
> القول الثاني : أن المراد بهذه الآية محمد ﵇ ، لأنه هو المفصل على الكل ، وإنما قال : * (ورفع بعضهم درجات) * على سبيل التنبيه والرمز كمن فعل فعلا عظيما فيقال له : من فعل هذا فيقول أحدكم أو بعضكم ويريد به نفسه ، ويكون ذلك أفخم من التصريح به ، وسئل الحطيئة عن أشعر الناس ، فذكر زهيراً والنابغة ، ثم قال : ولو شئت لذكرت الثالث أراد نفسه ، ولو قال : ولو شئت لذكرت نفسي لم يبق فيه فخامة
>
> "The second view is that this verse means Muhammad, since he is the one favored above all others. It says, “He raised some of them in ranks,” as a hint and an allusion. A person may do something great and be asked, “Who did this?” He may answer, “One of you,” or “Some of you,” while meaning himself. This sounds grander than naming himself directly. Al-Hutay'ah was asked who was the greatest poet. He named Zuhayr and al-Nabighah, then said, “If I wished, I could name the third.” He meant himself. Had he said, “If I wished, I could name myself,” the grandeur would have disappeared."


Al-Hutay'a, asked to name the greatest poet, names two rivals and leaves himself as "the third", and the grandeur survives precisely because he did not say "myself". Al-Razi records this as the reading of Qur'an 2:253, where "We raised some of them in degrees" alludes to the Prophet ﷺ in the third person. One speaker, presenting himself at a distance, is an Arabic art of self-magnification. When the Quran says "He" of Allah, it is using the same register the poets invented for themselves.

The rhetoricians gave the whole device a name and a taxonomy.

> [!tip]- al-Jurjani, al-Hashiya 'ala al-Kashshaf, p63
> وأشار بقوله (وقد التفت امرؤ القيس) إلى نوع رابع هو الانتقال من التكلم إلى الخطاب في ليلك واقتصر على هذه الأربعة لأنها أكثر الأنواع وأشهرها ... أما في علم المعاني فباعتبار كونه على خلاف مقتضي الظاهر . وأما في البيان فباعتبار أنه إيراد لمعنى واحد في طرق مختلفة الدلالة عليه جلاء وخلفاء وبهذين الاعتبارين يفيد الكلام حسنا ذاتيا للبلاغة . أما في البديع فمن حيث إن فيه جمعا بين صور متقابلة في معنى واحد فكان من المحسنات المعنوية ... فيكون ليلك التفاتا من التكلم إلى الخطاب
>
> "His words, “Imru al-Qays shifted,” point to a fourth type, the change from speaking in the first person to addressing someone directly in “your night.” He mentioned these four because they are the most common and famous types. In the science of meanings, this shift differs from what the situation normally requires. In rhetoric, it expresses one meaning through different ways that make it clearer and more vivid. These two aspects give speech its own beauty and eloquence. In literary embellishment, it joins opposite forms within one meaning, so it is a type of meaningful embellishment. Thus, “your night” shifts from the first person to direct address."


Iltifat, the turn. The rhetoricians classify the shifts, from speaking about to addressing, from first person to second, and they find their textbook example in Imru' al-Qays complaining of his own sleepless night as "your night". The shifts are not confusion. They are a named art with named beauties, and the Quran writes in a language whose poets had long practiced the art. The rhetoricians came later and named what the poets had been doing.

So the usage layer closes. The plural of majesty and the person-shift are both native to Arabic speech. The demand for a pre-Islamic king saying we of himself alone should also be measured against the opponent's own ground. The only divine plurals his canon carries are in-scripture, Genesis 1:26 and its companions. The only in-scripture plural-for-one the Quran needs is likewise inside the book, the dying soul's plea and the single Prophet addressed in the plural. A bar that the opponent's own evidence does not clear is not a bar the Quran has to clear. The question of codification cuts both ways. A rule read out of the Quran would explain the Quran perfectly and nothing else. This rule explains the poets, the kings, the dying soul's plea, and the book at once, and a rule that explains all of them was already in the language.

## 3. The Same Act in Two Pronouns

- **Source:** Ibn Shahrashub, Mutashabih al-Qur'an v2 p272; Bihar al-Anwar v16 p336
- **Question:** does the Quran's pronoun usage carry arithmetic
- **Claim:** the book uses plural forms for single referents, describes the same acts with We and with He, and names its co-agents whenever any act has them
- **Basis:** Qur'an 9:17, 49:4, 24:2, 50:24, 82:7, 95:4, 2:34, 33:56, 19:64, 97:1-4, 50:16, 15:9

If the We of the Quran counted speakers, the Quran would use its plurals only where referents are many. It does the opposite, and a Shia scholar of the twelfth century drew up the evidence.

### The Book's Own Plural for One

> [!tip]- Ibn Shahrashub, Mutashabih al-Qur'an, v2, p272
> لفظ جمع يراد به الواحد - ما كانَ لِلْمُشْرِكِينَ أَنْ يَعْمُرُوا مَساجِدَ اللَّهِ يعني المسجد الحرام - إِنَّ الَّذِينَ يُنادُونَكَ وهو رجل نادى يا محمد إن مدحي زين وإن شتمي شين - وَلْيَشْهَدْ عَذابَهُما طائِفَةٌ مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ الطائفة خرجت من حيز الواحد ودخلت في آخر - وفي التفسير واحد واثنان فما فوقهما - بِمَ يَرْجِعُ الْمُرْسَلُونَ وهو واحد يدل عليه قوله ارْجِعْ إِلَيْهِمْ ... أما قوله لمالك أَلْقِيا فِي جَهَنَّمَ ففي أخبار أهل البيت ع إن الخطاب للنبي ص وأمير المؤمنين ع وقال المبرد هذا فعل مثنى للتأكيد كأنه قال ألق ألق
>
> "A plural word may mean one person. "The idolaters must not maintain Allah's mosques" means the Sacred Mosque. "Those who call out to you" refers to one man who called, "Muhammad, my praise is beauty and my insult is disgrace." "Let a group of believers witness their punishment" leaves the register of the single one and enters another. In the commentary it can be one, two, or more. "See what the messengers return with" refers to one person, as shown by the words, "Return to them." As for His words to Malik, "Cast both of you into Hell," reports from the People of the House say that Allah addressed the Prophet and the Commander of the Faithful. Al-Mubarrad said this is a dual verb used for emphasis, as if He said, "Cast, cast.""


Ibn Shahrashub's catalogue of the Quran's plural forms with single referents. "The mosques of God" means the one Sacred Mosque. "Those who call you" is one caller. And the dual "cast, you two" the school reads as addressed to two, the Prophet ﷺ and Ali ﵇, while al-Mubarrad read it as a dual of emphasis, "cast, cast". A book that says the mosques for one mosque cannot be heard to count speakers in its pronouns. Its own grammar forbids the charge's arithmetic. The catalogue proves the point for plural forms in the third person. The first person is fixed by the grammarians' rule with the kings' custom.

The book also describes the same act with both pronouns, and the school's own literature moves between them without effort.

> [!note]- Manaqib Ibn Shahrashub, in Bihar al-Anwar, v16, p336
> مناقب ابن شهرآشوب : كان له اثنان وعشرون خاصية : كان أحسن الخلائق : " الذي خلقك فسواك (4) " وأجملهم : " لقد خلقنا الانسان في أحسن تقويم (5) "
>
> "From Manaqib Ibn Shahrashub. He had twenty-two special qualities. He was the finest of all creatures, “He created you and formed you well.” He was also the most beautiful of them, “We created man in the finest form.”"


One narration, proving the Prophet's ﷺ qualities, cites the creation of the fairest of creatures from the He of Qur'an 82:7 and the same creation from the We of Qur'an 95:4, side by side, and the commentators who cite them together sense no change of actor between them.

> [!quote]- Qur'an 82:7 and 95:4, as cited in Bihar al-Anwar, v16, p336
> الذي خلقك فسواك ... لقد خلقنا الانسان في أحسن تقويم
>
> *alladhi khalaqaka fa-sawwaka ... laqad khalaqna al-insana fi ahsani taqwim*
>
> "He created you and shaped you. We created the human being in the finest form."


Creation in He. Creation in We. And the same family of pairs runs through the breath of the spirit itself.

> [!quote]- Qur'an 38:71-72, Mukhtasar Majma' al-Bayan, v3, p151, with Qur'an 66:12, Majma' al-Bahrayn, v4, p116
> إِذْ قالَ رَبُّكَ لِلْمَلائِكَةِ إِنِّي خالِقٌ بَشَراً مِنْ طِينٍ . فَإِذا سَوَّيْتُهُ وَنَفَخْتُ فِيهِ مِنْ رُوحِي ... ونفخنا فيه من روحنا
>
> *idh qala rabbuka lil-mala'ikati inni khaliqun basharan min tin. fa-idha sawwaytuhu wa-nafakhtu fihi min ruhi ... wa-nafakhna fihi min ruhina*
>
> "When your Lord said to the angels, "I am creating a human being from clay. When I have formed him and breathed into him of My spirit..." And We breathed into him of Our spirit."


One kind of act, the breath of the spirit, and three grammatical persons divide it by register. The Lord said, the third person of relay. I am creating, and I breathed of My spirit, the first person of the giving, in Adam's making (with the same wording at Qur'an 15:29). And We breathed of Our spirit, the plural of majesty, in the making of Jesus within Mary (Qur'an 66:12). The Christian reader meets the We at the verse nearest his own theology, and the person it carries there is the same One who said I at Adam. One act, one God, two registers, and no commentator citing them together feels a seam.

### Where Helpers Exist, the Book Names Them

The charge asks whether anyone helps Allah. The book answers by grammar. When creatures share in an act, the Quran never hides them in a pronoun. It names them, coordinates them, and puts them under permission.

> [!quote]- Qur'an 2:34, as cited in al-Kafi, v1, p474
> وإذ قلنا للملائكة اسجدوا لآدم فسجدوا إلا إبليس أبى
>
> *wa-idh qulna lil-mala'ikati usjudu li-adama fa-sajadu illa Iblis. aba*
>
> "When We said to the angels, "Bow down before Adam," they bowed down except Iblis. He refused."


The angels are the addressees of "We said", never the co-speakers. The We commands, the angels hear, and the verse keeps the two ranks distinct by construction.

And the angels have a we of their own. The expert form of the charge cites verses where exegetes heard the angels inside the plural, and the strongest of them is Maryam.

> [!quote]- Qur'an 19:64, Mukhtasar Majma' al-Bayan, v2, p294
> وَما نَتَنَزَّلُ إِلَّا بِأَمْرِ رَبِّكَ لَهُ ما بَيْنَ أَيْدِينا وَما خَلْفَنا وَما بَيْنَ ذلِكَ وَما كانَ رَبُّكَ نَسِيًّا (64)
>
> *wa-ma natanazzalu illa bi-amri rabbika. lahu ma bayna aydina wa-ma khalfana wa-ma bayna dhalika. wa-ma kana rabbuka nasiyya*
>
> "We descend only by your Lord's command. To Him belongs what lies before us, what lies behind us, and what lies between them. Your Lord never forgets."


There the we is the angels' own voice, the Prophet ﷺ their addressee, and their Lord named in the third person with His command as their only warrant. The verse proves the discriminant. When the we is the angels', the book puts it in the angels' mouth and marks it by their Lord's command. When the we is Allah's, it stands alone and unmarked, as in the one sentence of Qur'an 6:99, where Allah sends down and We brings forth under one subject. Where the mufassirun, the Quran commentators, have heard the angels sharing in an act, they pointed to the verses that name them, the descent by permission (Qur'an 97:4) and the wings (Qur'an 35:1), and the plural of majesty is never left carrying them unmarked. The book tells its speakers apart by naming them, and this verse is where it does so.

> [!quote]- Qur'an 33:56, as printed in Majma' al-Bayan, v8, p179
> إن الله وملائكته يصلون على النبي ... يا أيها الذين آمنوا صلوا عليه وسلموا تسليما
>
> *inna Allaha wa-mala'ikatahu yusalluna 'ala al-nabi. ya ayyuha alladhina amanu sallu 'alayhi wa-sallimu taslima*
>
> "Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet. You who believe, send blessings upon him and greet him with peace."


When Allah and the angels share one verb, the verse names both parties in coordination, "Allah and His angels". The grammar of shared action is explicit naming, and this verse is its clearest form.

> [!quote]- Qur'an 97:1-4, Mukhtasar Majma' al-Bayan, v3, p574
> إِنَّا أَنْزَلْناهُ فِي لَيْلَةِ الْقَدْرِ (1) وَما أَدْراكَ ما لَيْلَةُ الْقَدْرِ (2) لَيْلَةُ الْقَدْرِ خَيْرٌ مِنْ أَلْفِ شَهْرٍ (3) تَنَزَّلُ الْمَلائِكَةُ وَالرُّوحُ فِيها بِإِذْنِ رَبِّهِمْ مِنْ كُلِّ أَمْرٍ (4)
>
> *inna anzalnahu fi laylati al-qadr. wa-ma adraka ma laylatu al-qadr. laylatu al-qadri khayrun min alfi shahr. tanazzalu al-mala'ikatu wa-al-ruhu fiha bi-idhni rabbihim min kulli amr*
>
> "We sent it down on the Night of Decree. What will make you understand what the Night of Decree is? The Night of Decree is better than a thousand months. The angels and the Spirit descend in it by their Lord's permission with every command."


The Night of Decree does both in one sura. The descent of the Quran is We in the first verse. The angels and the Spirit get their own verb in the fourth, "they descend, by their Lord's permission". The carriers are named, the permission is named, and the We stays the We.

> [!quote]- Qur'an 50:16, al-Jadwal fi I'rab al-Qur'an, v30, p52
> وَلَقَدْ خَلَقْنَا الْإِنْسانَ وَنَعْلَمُ ما تُوَسْوِسُ بِهِ نَفْسُهُ وَنَحْنُ أَقْرَبُ إِلَيْهِ مِنْ حَبْلِ الْوَرِيدِ
>
> *wa-laqad khalaqna al-insana wa-na'lamu ma tuwaswisu bihi nafsuh. wa-nahnu aqrabu ilayhi min habli al-warid*
>
> "We created the human being, and We know what his soul whispers to him. We are nearer to him than his jugular vein."


And nearness itself is said in both persons. "We are nearer to him than his jugular vein" is the We. "I am near" (Qur'an 2:186) is the I, as the reports below show. One nearness, two registers, and the pair proves the pronouns carry emphasis.

> [!quote]- Qur'an 15:9, as printed in al-Burhan fi Tafsir al-Qur'an, v3, p397
> إِنَّا نَحْنُ نَزَّلْنَا الذِّكْرَ وإِنَّا لَه لَحافِظُونَ
>
> *inna nahnu nazzalna al-dhikra wa-inna lahu la-hafizun*
>
> "We have sent down the Reminder, and We will surely preserve it."


"We, We sent down the Reminder, and We are its guardians." The doubled We of this verse is the charge's favorite target, and it sits in a book that names Jibril as the carrier of the same sending down (Qur'an 2:97), "upon your heart by Allah's permission", and names the Trustworthy Spirit (Qur'an 26:193) beside it. The sending is one. The We is Allah's. The carriers are named elsewhere, which is exactly where the book wants them.

The grammar layer closes. The Quran's own usage forbids reading number into its pronouns. The remaining question is where the We sits doctrinally, and the answer is next to the book's strictest oneness.

## 4. Where the We Meets the One God

- **Source:** Mukhtasar Majma' al-Bayan v3 p328; Majma' al-Bayan v9 p267; al-Mizan v18 p381; Tafsir al-Qummi v2 p448
- **Question:** does the We sit near partnership in the Quran's own arrangement
- **Claim:** the We appears inside the book's strongest assertions of oneness, and the school reads those passages as tawhid arguments
- **Basis:** Qur'an 51:47-51, 112

If the We carried any scent of partnership, the book would keep it away from its oneness passages. It does the opposite.

> [!quote]- Qur'an 51:47-51, Mukhtasar Majma' al-Bayan, v3, p328
> وَالسَّماءَ بَنَيْناها بِأَيْدٍ وَإِنَّا لَمُوسِعُونَ (47) وَالْأَرْضَ فَرَشْناها فَنِعْمَ الْماهِدُونَ (48) وَمِنْ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ خَلَقْنا زَوْجَيْنِ لَعَلَّكُمْ تَذَكَّرُونَ (49) فَفِرُّوا إِلَى اللَّهِ إِنِّي لَكُمْ مِنْهُ نَذِيرٌ مُبِينٌ (50) وَلا تَجْعَلُوا مَعَ اللَّهِ إِلهاً آخَرَ إِنِّي لَكُمْ مِنْهُ نَذِيرٌ مُبِينٌ (51)
>
> *wa-al-sama'a banaynaha bi-aydin wa-inna la-musi'un. wa-al-arda farashnaha fa-ni'ma al-mahidun. wa-min kulli shay'in khalaqna zawjayni la'allakum tadhakkarun. fa-firru ila Allahi inni lakum minhu nadhirun mubin. wa-la taj'alu ma'a Allahi ilahan akhara inni lakum minhu nadhirun mubin*
>
> "We built the heaven with strength, and We are surely expanding it. We spread out the earth, and how excellent are We at preparing it. We created every thing in pairs, so that you may remember. Flee to Allah. I am a clear warner to you from Him. Do not set up another god beside Allah. I am a clear warner to you from Him."


One passage, three persons. We built, We spread, We created pairs, then the passage breaks into "flee to Allah; I am a warner from Him", then "do not set up with Allah another god". The We lives next door to the first person and to the book's ban on partners. The school's commentators read the passage exactly so.

> [!tip]- al-Tabrisi, Majma' al-Bayan, v9, p267
> المعنى : ( والسماء بنيناها بأيد ) تقديره وبنينا السماء بنيناها بقوة ، عن ابن عباس ومجاهد وابن زيد وقتادة أي : خلقناها ورفعناها ، على حسن نظامها ( وإنا لموسعون ) أي قادرون على خلق ما هو أعظم منها ... ( والأرض فرشناها ) ... ( فنعم الماهدون ) نحن إذ فعلنا ذلك للمنافع ومصالح العباد ، لا لجر نفع ، ولا لدفع ضرر
>
> "The meaning of “We built the sky with strength” is, We built the sky with power. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Zayd, and Qatadah said this means that We created it and raised it in a fine order. “We are fully able” means that We can create what is greater than it. “We spread out the earth.” “How excellent are We at preparing it.” We did this for the benefit and welfare of people. We did not do it to gain benefit or prevent harm."


> [!tip]- al-Tabrisi, Mukhtasar Majma' al-Bayan, v3, p329
> ( وَالْأَرْضَ فَرَشْناها ) أي بسطناها ومهدناها لمنافع العباد وخلقنا من كل شيء صنفين مثل الليل والنهار ، والأرض والسماء ، والشمس والقمر ، والجن والإنس ، والبر والبحر ، وقيل : الزوجين الذكر والأنثى لكي تعلموا أن خالق هذه الأزواج واحد لا يشبهه أحد
>
> "We spread out the earth and prepared it for people's needs. We created everything in pairs, such as night and day, earth and sky, sun and moon, jinn and humans, and land and sea. It is also said that the pair means male and female, so that you may know that the Creator of these pairs is One and that nothing resembles Him."


Al-Tabrisi glosses the We-verses with the tawhid they serve, and his gloss on the pairs runs to the section's point. His short recension of the commentary states it as its own exhibit.

> [!tip]- al-Tabataba'i, al-Mizan, v18, p381
> ( بيان ) تشير الآيات إلى عدة من آيات الله الدالة على وحدانيته في الربوبية ورجوع أمر التدبير في الأرض والسماء والناس وأرزاقهم إليه ... والاستنتاج الآتي في آخر هذه الآيات في قوله : ( ففروا إلى الله - إلى أن قال - ولا تجعلوا مع الله إلها آخر ) الآية ، يشهد على أن سوق هذه الآيات والدلائل لاثبات وحدانيته تعالى في الربوبية
>
> "Explanation. The verses point to several signs of Allah that prove He alone governs all things. He directs the earth, the sky, people, and their provision. The conclusion at the end says, "Flee to Allah," then, "Do not set up another god with Allah." This shows that these verses and proofs establish that Allah alone rules and governs."


Al-Tabataba'i says the same with the school's full weight. The verses are marshaled to establish His oneness in lordship, and their conclusion is the flight to Allah and the ban on another god. The We is the register the book uses to argue oneness.

The sura of pure oneness answers in the He, the register of the Lord being taught, and its occasion of revelation was a question about lineage.

> [!note]- Tafsir al-Qummi, v2, p448
> سورة الاخلاص مكية آياتها خمس ط (بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم قل هو الله أحد) اي هو الله الأحد وكان سبب نزولها ان اليهود جاءت إلى رسول الله ﵌ فقالت : ما نسب ربك ؟ فأنزل الله (قل هو الله أحد الله الصمد لم يلد ولم يولد ولم يكن له كفوا أحد) ومعنى قوله : أحد أحدي النعت كما قال رسول الله ﵌ : نور لا ظلام فيه وعلم لا جهل فيه وقوله : الصمد ، اي الذي لا مدخل فيه وقوله : لم يلد ، اي لم يحدث ولم يولد ولم يكن له كفوا أحد ، قال : لا له كفو ولا شبيه ولا شريك ولا ظهير ولا معين .
>
> "Surat al-Ikhlas was revealed in Mecca. It has five verses. In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Say, 'He is Allah, the One.' The Jews came to the Messenger of Allah and asked, "What is your Lord's lineage?" Then Allah revealed, "Say, He is Allah, the One, Allah, the Everlasting Refuge. He did not beget, and He was not born. No one is equal to Him." Ahad means that His attributes are unique. The Messenger of Allah said, "He is a light free of darkness and knowledge free of ignorance." Al-Samad means the One with no opening within Him. "He did not beget" means that He did not bring anything into existence. "He was not born, and no one is equal to Him." He has no equal, no likeness, no partner, no supporter, and no helper."


The Jews asked the Prophet ﷺ, what is your Lord's lineage, and the answer was the sura of the One. The third person here is the presentation of Allah for others to learn of Him. And the gloss al-Qummi transmits closes the helpers question with five denials. No equal, no likeness, no partner, no backer, no helper. The sura that says He is the sura that denies every companion the charge hopes to find inside We.

This layer closes the plurality half of the charge. The We is majesty inside a book that banks its oneness beside it. The confusion half remains, the question of who speaks when the book says He, and the school's answer has three parts, a named device, a named relay, and a named occasion.

## 5. The Person-Shifts Have a Name

- **Source:** Kanz al-Daqa'iq v1 p118; al-Mizan v3 p377; Sharh Usul al-Kafi v1 p122 and v3 p204; al-Insaf v2 p174; Mukhtasar Majma' al-Bayan v1 p118; Bihar al-Anwar v18 p173
- **Claim:** the shifts of person in the Quran are the named device iltifat, used with stated purposes, and the He-passages are Allah's own speech carried by a named relay
- **Basis:** Qur'an 1:1-7, 2:168, 9:2, 2:186, 69:40

The scholarly form of the charge reads person-shifts as the seams of different authors. The shifts sit inside single sentences (Qur'an 6:99) and single passages (Qur'an 51:47-51), where different hands cannot hide, and the same act carries both pronouns (Qur'an 82:7 and 95:4).

The Fatiha performs the shift in its first five verses. Praise of the Lord of the worlds, all third person, then suddenly the address turns to You alone, second person, and the worshipper is standing before the One he was describing.

> [!tip]- al-Mashhadi, Kanz al-Daqa'iq, v1, p118
> وفي إيراد « إياك » دون « إياه » ، كما هو مقتضى الظاهر ، التفات من الغيبة إلى الخطاب . ومن النكتة الخاصة ، في الالتفات من الغيبة إلى الخطاب ، في هذا المقام ، بعد اشتماله على فائدة عامة ، من جهة المتكلم ، وهي التصرف والافتنان في وجود الكلام واظهار القدرة عليها ، ومن جهة المخاطب ، وهي تطرية نشاطه في سماع الكلام ، وايقاظه للإصغاء إليه . أنه لما قيل : « إياك » بدل « إياه » ، فقد نزل الغائب بواسطة أوصافه المذكورة التي أوجب تميزه وانكشافه ، حتى صار كأنه تبدل خفاء غيبته ، بجلاء حضوره ، منزلة المخاطب في التمييز والظهور
>
> "The use of iyyaka carries the speech from referring to someone absent into directly addressing Him. This shift has a general benefit. For the speaker, it shows skill and variety in expression. For the hearer, it renews attention and wakes the listener to hear carefully. Here it has a further purpose. The word iyyaka brings the One previously spoken of through His qualities into the position of one directly addressed. Those qualities distinguished Him and made Him known. The hiddenness of His absence became as clear as His presence. He therefore became like one directly addressed in clarity and distinction."


Al-Mashhadi explains the turn. From the Speaker's side it displays command of the speech. From the hearer's side it wakes attention. And the special benefit here is that the One described by His attributes becomes as if the obscurity of His absence exchanged itself for the clarity of presence. The shift moves the reciter from learning about Allah to addressing Him. It is the opposite of confusion. It is the prayer's engine.

The school's modern tafsir catalogs the device across the book.

> [!tip]- al-Tabataba'i, al-Mizan, v3, p377
> وأعلم أن في الآيات موارد من الالتفات من الغيبة إلى الخطاب ومن خطاب الجمع إلى خطاب المفرد وبالعكس وفيها موارد من وضع الظاهر موضع الضمير كتكرر لفظ الجلالة في عدة مواضع والنكتة في الجميع ظاهرة للمتأمل
>
> "Know that these verses include shifts from speaking about Allah to speaking directly to Him. They also shift between addressing many people and addressing one person. In some places, they use an explicit noun where a pronoun would usually appear, such as repeating the name Allah several times. A thoughtful reader can see the purpose of all these expressions."


Al-Tabataba'i notes the shifts in one passage after another, absence to address, plural to singular, pronoun to explicit noun, and says the purposes are clear to the reflecting reader. The hadith commentary of the school does the same work on the Quran and on the Imams' ﵈ own words.

> [!tip]- al-Mazandarani, Sharh Usul al-Kafi, v1, p122
> (فقال : إذا قيل لهم) الضمير للناس في قوله تعالى : (يا أيها الناس كلوا مما في الأرض حلالاً طيباً ولا تتبعوا خطوات الشيطان) على سبيل الالتفات من الخطاب إلى الغيبة للتنبيه على بعدهم عن رتبة الخطاب بسبب سلوكهم طريق التقليد
>
> "In the words, "When it is said to them," the pronoun refers to the people in Allah's words, "People, eat what is lawful and good on the earth. Do not follow Satan's footsteps." > [!tip]- al-Mazandarani, Sharh Usul al-Kafi, v3, p204
> (الذي لا يدركنا الغالي) الموصول صفة للنمط الأوسط وإفراده باعتبار اللّفظ والأصل أن يقول لا يدركه بالضمير للموصول إلاّ أنّه أتى بضمير المتكلّم من باب الالتفات من الغيبة إلى التكلّم للتصريح بالمقصود كما في قول أمير المؤمنين (﵇) : «أنا الّذي سمّتني أمي حيدرة»
>
> "In “the extremist cannot grasp us,” the relative pronoun describes the middle pattern. It is singular because of its wording. The original wording would be “cannot grasp him,” using a pronoun that refers back to the relative pronoun. The verse brings the first-person pronoun, a shift from the third person to the first. It states the intended meaning plainly, as Amir al-Muminin said, “I am the one my mother named Haydara.”"


One grammar for the book and the house. The Quran shifts from addressing "O mankind" to reporting "when it is said to them", to mark their distance from the rank of address. And Imam al-Rida ﵇ speaks of us, we the middle way whom the extremists cannot grasp, where the base grammar would say him, a shift from third person to first for the sake of stating the object openly, like Ali's ﵇ naming himself Ḥaydara, the one his mother so named. The Imams ﵈ use the device the Quran uses, which settles what kind of device it is.

The Sunni rhetorical tradition reaches the same verdict on the same terms.

> [!tip]- al-Iskandari, al-Insaf, v2, p174
> ثم التفات من التكلم إلى الغيبة بقوله - واعلموا أنكم غير معجزي الله وأن الله - وأصله واعلموا أنكم غير معجزي وأنى ، وفي هذا الالتفات بعد الالتفات الأول افتنان في أساليب البلاغة وتفخيم للشأن وتعظيم للأمر ... وكل هذا من حسنات الفصاحة
>
> "Then the speech turns from "We" to speaking about Allah by name in, "Know that you cannot escape Allah, and that Allah..." Its original form was, "Know that you cannot escape Me, and that I..." This shift, after the first shift, shows variety in eloquent expression. It gives the matter greater weight and importance. All of this belongs to the beauties of eloquence."


Al-Insaf, commenting on al-Zamakhshari, analyzes the shift of Qur'an 9:2 from the first person escape clause to the naming of Allah, and calls the turns virtuosity in the methods of eloquence, magnifying the station and the matter. The verse's base form is first person, and the shift to third is the art. That is the He-question answered in advance, centuries before the charge existed.

### The Relay Is Named

Who speaks when the book says He. Allah speaks, and the carriers are named. The clearest statement is the gloss on 69:40.

> [!tip]- al-Tabrisi's gloss, in Bihar al-Anwar, v18, p173
> وقال في قوله تعالى : " إنه لقول رسول كريم " أي إن القرآن قول رسول كريم على ربه وهو جبرئيل (﵇) ، وهو كلام الله أنزله على لسانه ، ثم وصف جبرئيل فقال : " ذي قوة " أي فيما كلف وامر به من العلم والعمل وتبليغ الرسالة ... " أمين " على وحي الله ورسالاته إلى أنبيائه
>
> "Regarding Allah's words, "It is truly the word of a noble messenger," he said that the Quran is the word brought by a noble messenger before his Lord, who is Jibril. It is Allah's speech, which He sent down through Jibril. Allah then describes Jibril, "Possessing strength," meaning strength in the knowledge, actions, and delivery of the message entrusted to him. "Trustworthy," meaning trustworthy with Allah's revelation and His messages to His prophets."


The Quran is the word of a noble messenger toward his Lord, Jibril ﵇, and it is Allah's speech sent down upon his tongue. Add the grammar of the qul-verses, where Allah composes the Prophet's ﷺ exact words, say to them that He is Allah, One, and the architecture is complete. Allah speaks, Jibril carries to the Prophet's ﷺ heart, the Prophet recites, and each layer is grammatically visible in the book. Third-person self-presentation plus named relay is the book's standing design.

### The Occasion of the I

One shift has a recorded occasion, and it prepares the next section.

> [!note]- from al-Hasan, in Mukhtasar Majma' al-Bayan, v1, p118
> روي عن الحسن أن سائلا سأل النبي ( ص ) أقريب ربنا فنناجيه أم بعيد فنناديه ؟ فنزلت الآية
>
> "Hasan reported that a questioner asked the Prophet, "Is our Lord near, so we may speak quietly to Him, or far, so we must call out to Him?" Then the verse came down."


A questioner asked the Prophet ﷺ whether the Lord is near, that they should whisper, or far, that they should call out. The answer came down without the relay marker. No command to say stands before the answer. The Lord Himself, in the first person, told him He is near, and that is the I of the Quran, the register of nearness and answer.

> المسألة الرابعة : إذا كان المقصود إثبات التوحيد ، فكيف قال : * ( بنيناها ) * ولم يقل بنيتها أو بناها الله ؟ نقول قوله : * ( بنينا ) * أدل على عدم الشريك في التصرف والاستبداد وقوله بنيتها يمكن أن يكون فيه تشريك ... فإذن علم أن المراد جمع التعظيم وأفاد النص عظمته ، فالعظمة أنفى للشريك فثبت أن قوله : * ( بنيناها ) * أدل على نفي الشريك من بنيتها وبناها الله .
> فإن قيل : لم قلت : إن الجمع يدل على التعظيم ؟ قلنا الجواب من الوجهين .
> الأول : أن الكلام على قدر فهم السامع ، والسامع هو الإنسان ، والإنسان يقيس الشاهد على الغائب ، فإن الكبير عندهم من يفعل الشيء بجنده وخدمه ولا يباشر بنفسه ، فيقول الملك فعلنا أي فعله عبادنا بأمرنا ويكون في ذلك تعظيم ، فكذلك في حق الغائب
>
> "Fourth question. If the aim is to establish God's oneness, why does He say, "We built it," and not, "I built it," or, "God built it"? We answer, "We built it" more clearly shows that no one shares His control or independent power. "I built it" may suggest a partnership. The intended meaning is therefore the plural of majesty. The wording shows His greatness. His greatness excludes any partner. Thus, "We built it" more clearly denies a partner than "I built it" or "God built it."

If someone asks, "Why do you say that the plural shows majesty?" We answer in two ways.

First, speech follows what the listener can understand. The listener is human. People compare what they see with what they cannot see. They consider great a ruler who acts through his armies and servants without acting personally. A king says, "We did it," meaning, "Our servants did it by our command." This gives him majesty. The same applies to the Unseen."


Al-Razi asks it exactly. If the aim is oneness, why does the verse say We built, and not I built. His answer inverts the charge. The We is more decisive against a partner than the I, because majesty itself excludes a sharer, and his explanation of the register is the king's we. Among the Arabs the great one acts through his household and servants, so the king says we did, meaning that his servants did it at his command, and there is magnification in it. The polemic reads the We as plurality. The tradition's own systematizer read it as the tawhid-intensive form.

> [!tip]- Abu Hayyan, al-Bahr al-Muhit, v7, p346
> والمخصوص بالمدح محذوف تقديره : فلنعم المجيبون نحن ، وجاء بصيغة الجمع للعظمة والكبرياء لقوله : * (فَقَدَرْنَا فَنِعْمَ الْقَادِرُونَ) *
>
> "The one praised is omitted. Its meaning is, "How excellent are We in answering." He used the plural form to show majesty and greatness, as in His words, "We determined, and how excellent are We at determining.""


> [!tip]- al-Alusi, Ruh al-Ma'ani, v12, p96
> والجمع للعظمة والكبرياء وفيه من تعظيم أمر الإجابة ما فيه ؛ وأخرج ابن مردويه عن عائشة رضي اللّه تعالى عنها قالت : «كان النبي صلّى اللّه عليه وسلم إذا صلى في بيتي فمر بهذه الآية وَلَقَدْ نادانا نُوحٌ فَلَنِعْمَ الْمُجِيبُونَ قال : صدقت ربنا أنت أقرب من دعا وأقرب من بغى فنعم المدعو ونعم المعطي ونعم المسؤول ونعم المولى أنت ربنا ونعم النصير»
>
> "The plural expresses majesty and greatness, and it gives the act of answering great importance. Ibn Marduyah reported from Aisha that whenever the Prophet prayed in her home and passed this verse, "Noah called upon Us, and how excellent are We in answering," he said, "You have spoken the truth, our Lord. You are nearer than the one who calls upon You, and nearer than the one who transgresses. How excellent are You to call upon, how excellent are You to give, how excellent are You to ask, how excellent are You as Master. You are our Lord, and how excellent are You as Helper.""


Abu Hayyan on 37:75 states it in a clause, that the plural is for greatness and majesty. Al-Alusi adds the report of the Prophet's ﷺ prayer at the same verse, confessing the Lord's truth and His nearness to every caller. The plural-of-majesty verse and the second-person prayer stand together in one report, We on the page and You on the tongue, and no one in the chain found confusion.

> [!tip]- al-Sha'rawi, Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, v5, p232
> فالأسلوب القرآني حين يأتي ب «إني» يشير إلى وحدة الذات ، وحين يأتي ب «إنا» يشير إلى تجمع صفات الكمال ... لذلك لا بد من ضمير التعظيم الذي يقول فيه النحويون : إن «نحن» و «نا» للمعظم نفسه . وقد عظم الحق نفسه ؛ لأن الأمر هنا حشد صفات يتطلبها إيجاد الكون والقيام على أمر الكون . ... فسبحان رب فوق كل مظنة * تعالى جلالا أن يحاط بذاته / إذا قال «إني» ذاك وحدة قدسه * وإن قال «إنّا» ذاك حشد صفاته
>
> "When the Quranic style says, "I," it points to the oneness of the Divine Being. When it says, "We," it points to the gathering of perfect qualities. Therefore, the pronoun of majesty is necessary. Grammarians say that "We" and "Us" refer to the One who is great. The Truth has declared His own greatness because creating the universe and governing it require a gathering of attributes.

Glory be to a Lord beyond every assumption. His majesty is too high for His Being to be fully understood. When He says, "I," that expresses the oneness of His holiness. When He says, "We," that expresses the gathering of His attributes."


The modern tradition keeps the same reading. Al-Sha'rawi states the division of registers, the I for the oneness of the Essence, the We for the gathering of the attributes of perfection, and cites the grammarians' rule that the plural pronouns belong to the one magnifying himself. Whether one frames the We as majesty or as the attributes in act, the frame is register, and register does not count. And the register itself answers the Trinity's form of plurality. Attributes gathered in one essence are what the One has. Persons are who the One is. The Quran's We gathers the first and never divides the second.

The corroboration layer closes. Lexicon, usage, the book's own naming, the school's tafsir, the school's hadith, and the opponent's own commentators agree. 

## 8. The Christian Canon on the Divine We

- **Holders cited:** Augustine of Hippo, On the Trinity I.7.14; the Council of Nicaea, 325
- **Scripture:** Genesis 1:26 and Deuteronomy 6:4, Westminster Leningrad Codex, Van Dyck Arabic, King James Version
- **Claim:** the Christian canon puts plural forms in God's mouth beside the strictest monotheism, and the church's reading of its own plural is creedal, not lexical

The method of the charge, reading a divine plural as plurality of agents, is the method Christians apply to Genesis.

> [!quote]- Genesis 1:26, Westminster Leningrad Codex, King James Version
> וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֱלֹהִ֔ים נַֽעֲשֶׂ֥ה אָדָ֛ם בְּצַלְמֵ֖נוּ כִּדְמוּתֵ֑נוּ
>
> *va-yomer elohim na'aseh adam be-tsalmenu ki-demutenu*
>
> "And God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness."

> [!quote]- Deuteronomy 6:4, Westminster Leningrad Codex, King James Version
> שְׁמַ֖ע יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֵ֖ינוּ יְהוָ֥ה ׀ אֶחָֽד
>
> *shema yisra'el YHWH elohenu YHWH echad*
>
> "Hear, O Israel, the LORD our God is one LORD."

The same canon that says "let us make man in our image" also says that the LORD our God is one LORD, and says that the man has become as one of us (Genesis 3:22), bids us go down (Genesis 11:7), and asks who will go for us (Isaiah 6:8), where the I and the us share one sentence. Genesis 3:22 works like Maryam's we, set grammar implying a court around the speaker, and the heavenly-court reading carries it without a council of gods. Whichever reading is adopted, the Trinity's or the majesty's, must carry all of these verses alike. Augustine reads the Genesis plural as the Son's presence in creation, in On the Trinity I.7.14, arguing that were the Father alone to have made man without the Son, the plural of Genesis 1:26 would never have been written. The Council of Nicaea in 325 confessed one God the Father Almighty, maker of all things, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom all things were made, God from God, of the same substance as the Father.

The comparison runs on four named tests. First, what each view asks a believer to accept about God. Second, whether each reading coheres with its own scripture. Third, which reading fits the words themselves. Fourth, which demands less of the text.

On the first test, each reading must square with its own scripture's monotheism, and both books hold the pair, plural forms and strict oneness, without dissolving either. On the second, the Quranic reading is a rule of the language the book speaks, settled by dictionaries, grammars, and usage, while the Trinitarian reading of Genesis reads the fourth-century creed back into Hebrew written a millennium before it. The synagogue's classic commentary reads the plural another way, as God consulting his heavenly court (Rashi on Genesis 1:26), and that reading is as old as the dispute.

On the third test, the words themselves. Augustine argues from the plural pronouns to plurality of persons, so the number of the pronoun is the load-bearing point, and the Hebrew grammar gives it no such freight. The noun of God stands under singular agreement, and Deuteronomy above shows a plural noun of God standing under one LORD, with nobody reading the morphology as a census. Genesis 1:26's verb is plural in form, like the Arabic nahnu, and that case is carried by the royal we of English, the queen's we are under one speaker, which is the point already made. On the fourth test, the plural of majesty needs no extra persons and no creed to import them, while the Trinitarian reading needs Nicaea to decide what the us means. The strongest form of the remaining objection deserves its name. Read the king's we as executors hidden inside the pronoun, and the divine We becomes Allah with his angels as his retinue. The note has already answered what that reading is worth. The book names the retinue wherever it acts, and the named retinue are creatures under command, worshippers who descend by permission and salute the Prophet ﷺ, which is not the plurality the charge wants. The charge needs helpers of the divine act who share the act's rank. The book gives creatures who carry out the act of the One. The grammar of majesty and the rule that names its co-agents together leave the retinue standing only as what has already been named, creatures under command, with nothing between creature and Creator inside the pronoun.

The agreement question has its own one-line answer. The English monarch says we are, and never we is, one speaker under plural agreement, and Latin grammarians gave the rule its name, pluralis majestatis. Plural agreement under a single will is the royal we's grammar in every language that has it, Arabic included, and the Hebrew noun of God under singular predicates shows the neighboring Semitic grammar carrying the same load.

The sophisticated form of the Christian reading does not rest on the pronoun at all. It reads Genesis through John's prologue, all things made through him, and through Paul's by him all things were created. That reading carries its agent into the Hebrew from outside it, and the four tests above measure exactly that move. The pronoun charge is the popular form of the case, and the creedal form rests on the creed. A method that convicts the Quran's We convicts Genesis first, and applied with one standard it convicts neither.

The Islamic case has stood throughout on the dictionaries, the poets, the book's own usage, the school's tafsir, the hadith of the Ahl al-Bayt ﵈, and the opponent's own commentators. The comparison shows the charge's method failing on its home ground. That is the difference between a reading drawn from the language and a reading required by the creed.

## Final Verdict

The charge asked three questions, and the record answers each.

Does We mean others help Allah. No. Arabic has a plural of majesty, and the Kufan school's founding layer, al-Farra's, already reads it with the Quran's own verses as the textbook cases, in both directions, God saying We and Our of Himself and a creature addressing the one God in a plural. Abu Ali, two centuries on, states it as too famous in the language to need proof. The poets and kings used it, the Prophet ﷺ used it, the Imams ﵈ used it, and the Quran itself uses plural forms for single referents where no theology is at stake at all. Where helpers truly exist, the book names them, Allah and His angels, the angels and the Spirit by their Lord's permission, and keeps the We to itself. And the school's own reading of 5:55 rests on this grammar, so within the tradition the rule stands at the foundation.

When the Quran says He, who is speaking. Allah is speaking, presenting Himself in the third person the way the rhetoricians name and the Imams ﵈ practice, and the words travel a named relay. The Quran is Allah's speech placed on the tongue of a noble messenger, Jibril ﵇, carried to the Prophet's ﷺ heart, recited by the Prophet, taught to the servant. The say-verses make the relay visible, and the qudsi Fatiha makes all three persons audible in one report.

Why does the book move between We, He, and I. Because the registers do different work, and the language has a device for moving between them. The We carries majesty in creation and sending down. The He presents the Lord for the servant to learn of Him. The I answers where nearness and mercy are promised, and at Qur'an 2:186 the relay command is dropped so the Lord answers the questioner Himself. The shifts have a name, iltifat, a taxonomy, and stated purposes, and the sermon and prayer life of the Ahl al-Bayt ﵈ run on the same grammar.

The method that reads number into these pronouns would convict Genesis before it reaches the sura of the Reminder. Held to one standard, the We is majesty, the He is presence taught, and the I is the Lord answering, and the helpers the charge went looking for are exactly where the Quran put them, named, permitted, and creatures. And the burden runs the other way. The charge needs the plural to carry number, and every theologically neutral token in the book, the mosques, the callers, the single Prophet addressed in the plural, testifies that it does not.

A reader who abandons the pronoun and retreats to the creed, the Son through whom all things were made, has conceded the pronoun case. The Genesis likeness is the comparison the method itself draws when one grammar is held to both canons, and on that ground the dictionaries stand with the Quran. The creedal case begins at Nicaea, and it must be argued from there, on its own ground.

blocks.text: Why the Quran Says We, He, and I

The charge comes in two forms, and both travel widely. The first asks it as arithmetic. Your book says We created you, We sent down the Reminder, We built the heaven. A plural speaker is plural, so who are the others helping Allah? The second asks it as confusion. The same book keeps switching between We, He, and I, sometimes inside one passage, and a speaker who knows who he is does not keep changing his own pronouns.

Both forms assume one thing, that an Arabic pronoun counts its referents the way an English pronoun does. It does not. Arabic has a standing rule for the exalted speaker, the plural of majesty, and the rule is printed in the grammar books, alive in the poets, and used by the Quran itself for single referents of no theological weight at all. When the Quran means that others act alongside Allah, it names them. When it wants the nearness of answer, it drops the relay and speaks as I. When it describes the Lord for the servant to learn, it says He. One Speaker, and many rooms of speech.

Premise 1: Arabic grammar itself lets one exalted speaker say we of himself alone. Al-Farra, the founder of the Kufan school who died in 207, reads the dying soul's plural to the one God as the Arabs' standing plural for one, set beside the Quran addressing the single Prophet in a plural verb. Al-Tusi's al-Tibyan states it as the linguists' answer and relays al-Khalil ibn Ahmad, the founder of Arabic grammar, declining to force a parse on that same plural because it is a plural. Al-'Ukbari's grammar of the Quran reads that verse the same way, with the divine We of Qur'an 15:9 as the parallel. The Shia school states the rule on its own ground, 5:55, where a plural in form has one referent, Ali ﵇ alone. Premise 2: The usage was alive among the Arabs. Imru' al-Qays says we are the kings and sons of kings. Al-Razi explains the register from the ground up; among the Arabs the great one acts through his household and retinue, so the king says we did, and there is magnification in it. The Prophet ﷺ says we, the company of the prophets. The Imams ﵈ say we of themselves and their house in what the school transmits, and their commentators explain that we with the same device the Quran's shifts use. Premise 3: The Quran keeps its own naming. It describes the same creation with He in Qur'an 82:7 and with We in Qur'an 95:4, and one hadith proving the Prophet's ﷺ beauty cites both verses side by side. It uses plural forms for single referents elsewhere, a catalogue Ibn Shahrashub drew up from the Quran itself. Where creatures share an act with Allah's permission, the Quran names them, Allah and His angels, the angels and the Spirit by their Lord's permission, and the angels as the addressees, never co-speakers. Premise 4: The shifts of person are a named device of Arabic eloquence, iltifat, with stated purposes, and the school's own commentary assigns those purposes verse by verse. The Imams ﵈ use the same device in their own speech, and the qudsi reports show Allah answering the servant in His own I where nearness and answer are being promised.

Conclusion: if the plural of majesty is ordinary Arabic, and the Quran uses plural forms for single referents and names its co-agents when it has them, then the We carries greatness and never number, and no helper hides inside it. If the person-shifts are a named device the Imams ﵈ themselves use, then the alternation of We, He, and I follows design. The charge survives only by reading an Arabic pronoun as an English census, and that method would convict Genesis and its let-us-make-man verse before it touches the sura of the Reminder.

blocks.text: 1. The Grammar of the Exalted We

Source: al-Farra, Ma'ani al-Qur'an v2 pp13, 241-242 and v3 p42; al-Tusi, al-Tibyan v7 p394; al-'Ukbari, al-Tibyan fi I'rab al-Qur'an p274; Abu al-Salah al-Halabi, Taqrib al-Ma'arif p188 Question: may one speaker of Arabic say we of himself alone Claim: the grammar of Arabic has a standing plural of majesty, and it runs in both directions, up to God and down from kings Basis: the grammarians' verdicts on Qur'an 23:99, 15:9, 23:12, and 6:99, and the school's reading of 5:55

The charge rests on one grammatical assumption, that a pronoun counts its referents. Arabic breaks that assumption before the Quran is even opened. The language has a plural of majesty, a we that one exalted speaker says of himself alone, and the rule is printed in the grammar books with the Quran's own We as the textbook example.
The Verdict of the Grammarians

al-Tusi, al-Tibyan, v7, p394 والثاني - انه جرى على تعظيم الذكر في خطاب الواحد بلفظ الجمع لعظم القدر كما يقول ذلك المتكلم ، قال الله تعالى " انا نحن نزلنا الذكر وانا له لحافظون " (1) وقال " ولقد خلقنا الانسان " (2) وما جرى مجراه . وروى النضر بن سمأل قال : سئل الخليل عن قوله " رب ارجعون " ففكر ثم قال : سألتموني عن شئ لا أحسنه ولا أعرف معناه ، والله أعلم ، لأنه جمع ، فاستحسن الناس منه ذلك "The second view is that one person is addressed with a plural form to honor the greatness of the one mentioned. A speaker may say this. Allah says, “We sent down the Reminder, and We will preserve it.” He also says, “We created man,” and similar expressions. Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl reported that Khalil was asked about the words, “My Lord, send me back.” He thought for a while and said, “You asked me about something I do not know how to explain, and I do not know its meaning. Allah knows best, since it is plural.” People admired this answer."

So the school's senior classical commentator fixes the rule first. The speech of one speaker can run in the plural form for greatness of station, and he says this is simply how speakers of Arabic talk. His parallel is the charge's own target, the doubled We of the Reminder verse (Qur'an 15:9). The report he relays cuts both ways, and the honest reading records both edges. Al-Khalil ibn Ahmad, a founder of Arabic grammar, was asked about the plural of the dying soul's plea in Qur'an 23:99, send them back, addressed to the one God. He declined to force a parse and said he does not know its analysis, because it is a plural, and the people of his circle found the reserve good. A reader who wants an anomaly can read the reserve his way, and the page does not hide the reserve. The founder's own stated reason is form-side, because it is a plural, and the Kufan school answered him within a generation. That reading is quoted below. The rule of al-Tusi is the tradition's settled answer, the plural of rank where the founder paused, and it runs in both directions, a creature addressing the one God in the plural and God speaking of Himself in it, with neither direction carrying number.
The grammar of the Quran reaches the same verdict in the same breath.
